Introduction to es4all

es4all.Rmd

The dominance family of effect sizes

For two groups, let d1,2d_{1,2} be the probability that a randomly drawn observation from group 1 is greater than a randomly drawn observation from group 2, d2,1d_{2,1} the probability of the reverse, and d0d^0 the probability of a tie (d1,2+d2,1+d0=1d_{1,2}+d_{2,1}+d^0=1). Any effect size built from these three comparison probabilities is dominance-based. es4all reports the following members of the family:

Effect size Abbrev. Definition Also known as
Stochastic difference SD d1,2−d2,1d_{1,2}-d_{2,1} Cliff’s delta, Glass rank-biserial correlation, net benefit; = risk difference (RD) for binary data
Adjusted stochastic difference ASD (d1,2−d2,1)/(d1,2+d2,1)(d_{1,2}-d_{2,1})/(d_{1,2}+d_{2,1}) Goodman and Kruskal’s gamma; = Yule’s Q for binary data
Number needed to treat NNT 1/(d1,2−d2,1)1/(d_{1,2}-d_{2,1}) reciprocal of risk difference; binary data only
Dominance D d1,2d_{1,2} Common language effect size (CLES), Grissom and Kim’s probability of superiority
Measure of stochastic superiority MSS d1,2+0.5d0d_{1,2}+0.5\,d^0 Vargha and Delaney’s A
Adjusted dominance AD d1,2/(d1,2+d2,1)d_{1,2}/(d_{1,2}+d_{2,1}) -
Generalized odds ratio GOR d1,2/d2,1d_{1,2}/d_{2,1} Agresti’s generalized odds ratio, win ratio; = odds ratio (OR) for binary data; = odds for continuous data
Win odds WO (d1,2+0.5d0)/(d2,1+0.5d0)(d_{1,2}+0.5\,d^0)/(d_{2,1}+0.5\,d^0) odds form of MSS
Standardized mean difference SMD 2Φ−1(d1,2)\sqrt{2} \Phi^{-1}(d_{1,2}) Cohen’s d; continuous data only

For discrete (binary or ordinal) data, an important property of the effect size is whether it is equivalence dependent. SD, MSS, WO, and NNT are equivalence dependent: their attainable range narrows as the probability of a tie grows, making them shrink toward the point of no effect. See the binary-data example below for an illustration of why this is a desirable property.

Functions

Function Data type Estimation
d_cont() Continuous (normal) Maximum likelihood (MLE)
d_bin() Binary MLE
d_ord() Ordinal MLE
d_one() Continuous, one-sample MLE
d_pair() Continuous, paired MLE
d_np() Any (continuous, binary, or ordinal) Non-parametric (distribution-free)

Each d_*() function accepts known distribution parameters, sample summary statistics, or record-level microdata as input.

Examples

Continuous data 

library(es4all)

set_opts(es = NA) prints all effect sizes (the default), while set_opts(es = c("D", "SD", ...)) prints a chosen subset.

set_opts(es = c("D", "SD"))
#> * Effect size: print the following effect sizes: D, SD.
d_cont(comparison_data$stature2)

Why equivalence dependence matters

This is the myocardial infarction (MI) example that has been discussed in the effect size literature.

set_opts(es = c("SD", "GOR"))
#> * Effect size: print the following effect sizes: SD, GOR.
d_bin(comparison_data$MI)
Data
What Value
Input comparison_data$MI
Groups Aspirin vs Placebo
Proportion (# Events / # Trials) the proportion of Aspirin who had the event was 0.9% (104/11037); the proportion of Placebo who had the event was 1.7% (189/11034)
Data k1=104k_1 = 104, n1=11037n_1 = 11037; k2=189k_2 = 189, n2=11034n_2 = 11034
About
What Value
About Aspirin for the prevention of myocardial infarction (MI)
Source Rosnow, R. L., & Rosenthal, R. (1989). Statistical procedures and the justification of knowledge in psychological science. American Psychologist, 44(10), 1276-1284. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.44.10.1276 (Table 2); and Ellis, P. D. (2010). The Essential Guide to Effect Sizes: Statistical Power, Meta-Analysis, and the Interpretation of Research Results. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511761676 (Table 1.4)
Notes Reported Pearson correlation coefficient r = 0.034. Based on binomial effect size display (BESD), reported percentage point reduction in heart attacks: 3.4 pp
Results: Stochastic difference (SD)
What Value
Effect size Stochastic difference (SD)
Result SD (Placebo vs. Aspirin) = 0.01 (95% CI: 0-0.01); p-value: < .001
Meaning The correlation between group (Placebo vs. Aspirin) and outcome is 0.01.
Equivalence dependence Equivalence dependent. This effect size’s possible range narrows toward the point of probabilistic equality (no effect) as the probability of a tied outcome grows, so it correctly reports a small effect when most pairs would have the same outcome regardless of the group. This is a desirable property in many settings, including the treatment and control group setting, since ties are part of the answer, not a nuisance to be divided out.
Other names Glass rank-biserial correlation; net benefit; Cliff’s delta; simple difference formula. SD = one of the two values of Somers’ Delta. |SD| = Freeman’s theta. For binary variables, SD = risk difference (RD), also known as excess risk, attributable risk, absolute risk increase / reduction (ARI / ARD).
Results: Generalized odds ratio (GOR)
What Value
Effect size Generalized odds ratio (GOR)
Result GOR (Placebo vs. Aspirin) = 1.8 (95% CI: 1.4-2.3); p-value: < .001
Meaning The odds ratio for Placebo vs. Aspirin is 1.8.
Equivalence dependence Not equivalence dependent. This effect size’s range does not depend on the probability of a tie, because tied pairs are divided out and only the pairs that are distinguishable are measured. It can therefore portray a relationship as large even when ties are common.
Other names Agresti’s generalized odds ratio for stochastic dominance; win ratio. For binary variables, GOR = odds ratio (OR). For continuous variables, GOR = odds.
Inference
What Value
Inference The result is statistically significant (p-value: < .001 < 0.05).
Side The effect is in favor of the event being more likely for Placebo than for Aspirin.
Methods
What Value
Methods Please include this or similar in your Methods section: We present [effect size name], a dominance-based effect size for binary variables, calculated using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), along with its 95% confidence interval and p-value. Results were considered to be statistically significant if p < 0.05. Data analyses were performed using the R package “es4all” (version 0.9.0).

The equivalence-dependent SD is tiny (0.01) because almost all pairs of patients tie on the outcome (“had an MI” vs. “did not have an MI”), while the equivalence-independent GOR (1.8) describes a much larger effect among the pairs that are actually distinguishable. These descriptions answer different questions – SD the population-wide question a treatment decision turns on, GOR the narrower question of how one-sided the comparison is among the pairs that differ.

Ordinal data

Analysis of data from the 1948 trial of streptomycin for the treatment of tuberculosis.

set_opts(es = NA) # restore the default (print all effect sizes)
#> * Effect size: print all effect sizes.
d_ord(comparison_data$TB)

Built-in example datasets

es4all comes with several datasets from published studies, used throughout its documentation and reproduced in the paper’s examples:

ret = NULL
for (nn in names(comparison_data)) {
  r1 = data.frame(Label = nn
    , About = strtrim( attr(comparison_data[[nn]], "meta")$About, 25)
    , `Group 1` = comparison_data[[nn]]$group[1]
    , `Group 2` = comparison_data[[nn]]$group[2]
    , Source = strtrim( attr(comparison_data[[nn]], "meta")$Source, 25)
    , check.names = FALSE)
  ret = rbind(ret, r1)
}
print(ret)
#>          Label                     About          Group 1         Group 2

Customizing output 

set_opts(
  conf.level = 0.95,  # confidence level of the interval
  es = NA,            # which effect sizes to print: NA (all, default) or a vector of names
  output = "auto",    # "auto", "huxtable", "gt", "kableExtra", "flextable", "screen", "Excel", "Word", "CSV"
  raw = FALSE         # if TRUE, return the raw intermediate data.frame instead of formatted output
)
#> * Level of confidence interval = 0.95 (significance level = 0.05).
#> * Effect size: print all effect sizes.
#> * Printing with huxtable for screen, gt for HTML, or kableExtra for PDF.
#> * Raw output: FALSE.
show_opts()
#> * Level of confidence interval = 0.95 (significance level = 0.05).
#> * Effect size: print all effect sizes.
#> * Printing with huxtable for screen, gt for HTML, or kableExtra for PDF.
#> * Raw output: FALSE.

output = "auto" selects huxtable for the console, gt for HTML, or kableExtra for PDF/LaTeX. "Excel", "Word", and "CSV" write to a file (pass file = "...") and require the openxlsx2 (for Excel) or flextable + officer (for Word) packages.
